Case Vignette: "Lukas"

Lukas is a 25-year-old salesperson who has been in a relationship with his girlfriend, Mia, for three years. He presents as clean-cut and articulate, but his eyes carry a hollow vigilance that never quite softens, even when he attempts a smile.

The trauma occurred two years ago, during a brief period when Lukas was visiting extended family in a region that suddenly became a war zone. What began as a two-week holiday to reconnect with his grandparents became a six-week nightmare of shelling, street fighting, and a desperate escape. The event that haunts him most happened on the tenth day. He and his cousin were walking to a market that had reportedly been safe. Without warning, a mortar round struck a building twenty meters ahead. The blast threw Lukas to the ground. When he stood up, his cousin was gone. In his place was a pile of rubble, a single sneaker, and a spreading pool of blood. Lukas spent the next three hours digging with his bare hands, under sporadic gunfire, until soldiers forced him away. His cousin’s body was never recovered.

In the immediate aftermath, Lukas felt nothing. He describes himself as “a machine,” methodically helping his family gather documents, find transport, and cross borders. He did not cry. He did not sleep. He simply moved. It was only after he returned to his home city, six weeks later, that the world began to splinter.

Now, two years later, Lukas works in high-end electronics sales. He is excellent at his job—charming, persistent, and able to read a customer’s hesitation. But the job is a performance. He describes walking onto the sales floor as “putting on a suit of armor.” The moment a customer raises their voice, or a door slams in the back room, or a child screams in the mall hallway, the armor cracks. His heart hammers. His vision tunnels. He sees the red sneaker. He has excused himself to the break room five times in the past month, locking the bathroom stall and pressing his forehead to the cold tile until his breathing slows.

His relationship with Mia is strained. He loves her, but he cannot be present. At night, he startles awake at 3:17 AM—the exact time the mortar hit, though he did not look at a clock until hours later. He thrashes, sometimes shouting, and has accidentally struck Mia in his sleep. She has learned to sleep in the guest room. During the day, he avoids crowds, loud noises, and any news coverage of conflict. He cannot watch movies with war scenes, even fictional ones. Last week, a car backfired outside his apartment, and he dove behind the couch, knocking over a lamp. He stayed there for ten minutes, shaking, while Mia tried to coax him out.

Lukas is constantly on edge. He scans every room for exits. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He cannot tolerate the smell of dust or the sound of helicopters. He has stopped visiting his own extended family, because the sight of his grandmother’s house—a replica of the one he fled—triggers flashbacks so vivid he can taste the grit of rubble in his mouth.

He feels profoundly guilty. He tells himself he should have saved his cousin. He replays the moment in loops, searching for a different decision, a faster reaction. He has stopped going to the gym, stopped seeing friends, stopped cooking—activities that once defined him. He says he feels “dead inside,” but his body is screaming. He drinks three to four beers most nights to dull the hypervigilance enough to sleep. He scored 76 on the PCL-5, a score reflecting severe PTSD symptoms across all clusters.

Lukas came to therapy because Mia gave him an ultimatum: get help, or she would leave. He does not want to lose her. But he also does not believe he deserves to feel better. He sits in the chair, hands clasped, and waits for someone to tell him what to do, because for two years, his own mind has been the only war zone he cannot escape.
